I am looking at the price where Euro collapsed and asking myself why the market decided that price was too expensive. More importantly, I am interested in observing what that decision looks like on screen. I can see that the Euro fell from there, but the market does not pay for noticing things in hindsight. The market pays when we correctly anticipate what may happen in the future and we are rewarded for our ability to act on that in a well risk defined manner. However, in order to do this, we need to know at what places we should to be paying attention, perched ready to pounce.

Prior to the collapse there was a rally and a base (see post #8 above). In the base the market was making a decision. The market was deciding if price was too cheap or too expensive. If the market decides price is too cheap, we will see a rally-base-rally develop. If the market decides price is too expensive, we will see rally-base-drop. It turns out we had a rally-base-drop, but that was only seen after that fact.

The weekly chart shows important decisions were made around this price level in the past.

The daily chart is more insightful, showing with more clarity the decisions being made around this price.

The 4hr chart shows the level being crossed up and down numerous times.

The 1hr chart shows some historical significance at this price level. The last time was around the 10th of October. I will take a closer look and see what happened at this time.

The 5min chart shows the market making decisions. The market decides price was too cheap on the 11th of October. The challenge I have is that I can see these decisions playing out at all different price levels on the chart. As mentioned, this is all in hindsight and I cannot trade in hindsight.

To me, the most useful piece of information on the chart, and what I would most likely be looking at in real time is the most recent demand marked in the green box. I say this as it just sticks out so clearly. When price reached this level, the market considered the Euro as cheap and there was strong demand for the Euro at this price. On the last test of the level, the demand was very strong and price zoomed away. The demand created a traditional support level.

What catches my eye was is fact that price moved away abruptly on testing the level. That is, the market did not wallow around at this price making a decision on the value of the Euro. The smart money had decided well before the Euro reached this price that it was cheap and the buy orders were eagerly waiting price to reach that level.

The question is, when prices comes back to that level again, what will happen? Will there still be demand at that price. If so, how much? If there is demand, the price will move up once again. However, there is only a finite amount of demand for a commodity at certain price. Once all the buyers have made their purchase, the demand disappears. The market is big, but it is still finite. Once the buyers have had their fill, the demand will have been all consumed.

When the Euro comes back to the level, price bases. That is, it forms a drop-base structure. Price did not zoom away. It’s during that base the a decision is being made. Is price still cheap? Or, is it now too expensive? It's time to decide? This is what the decision making process looks like zoomed out.

And this is what it looks like zoomed in.

The market decides price is too expensive. All the demand is consumed. Price falls away, leaving fresh supply. In the decision making process, what I see on screen is a S/R flip.

When price comes back to a S/R flip zone, a place where market changed its mind on the value of the Euro, that is the price at which the Euro collapsed. It's somewhere I should be looking at. In this case, it was a place where there was prior demand. But once that demand was consumed, what was left was fresh supply.
